newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanese court strikes down elections.
newsitem.headline: Lebanese court strikes down elections.

text.p: Lebanon's Constitutional Council, in an unprecedented decision, on Monday struck down the election of four parliamentary deputies including a government minister and ordered new elections for their seats, a court source said.
It was the first time in Lebanon's history that parliamentary elections have been struck down by a court or any other agency.

The court accepted four out of the 19 appeals lodged by defeated candidates after last summer's general elections which were criticised by independent observers, opposition politicians and the Lebanese media for alleged coercion, intimidation, bribery and fraud, the source said.
The 128 deputies elected to the parliament -- divided 50-50 between Christians and Moslems -- were overwhelmingly supporters of the pro-Syrian government.
Interior Minister Michel al-Murr told reporters the four seats would be vacant from Tuesday and by-elections would be held to fill them within 60 days.

The four who lost their seats included Fawzi Hobeish, a Maronite Christian who has been minister of culture and higher education in the government of billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri since the elections.

The appeal against Hobeish's election in the northern region of Akkar, beside the Syrian border, was lodged by Mikhael Daher, a prominent Maronite opposition politician who told the court an unnamed intelligence service -- apparently Syrian -- had intervened in the election in Hobeish's favour.

The other deposed deputies were Khaled Daher of Jamaa Islamiye (Islamic Group), a Sunni Moslem fundamentalist movement, Henri Shdeid, a Maronite elected as an ally of Hizbollah (Party of God), a Shi'ite fundamentalist group, and Emile Nawfal, a Maronite independent.
The source said the council's rulings would be officially announced after parliament, the interior ministry, the deputies involved and the appelants were informed of the results.

The rulings were the first assessments given on a Lebanese election by the Constitutional Council formed in 1994 and cannot be appealed. It had studied 40,000 documents of evidence in the 19 cases for seven months.

However, the appeals process has been mired in controversy since April 3 when council president Wajdi al-Mallat resigned in what legal sources and the media said was a protest against political pressure exercised on the court.

The sources said the judges were deeply divided and the court was under pressure to rule only on cases involving simple vote-counting errors, ignoring those involving allegations of fraud and coercion in favour of pro-government candidates.
Several petitions involving alleged fraud and intimidation were lodged by Christian opposition candidates.
The appeals against three of the deputies deposed by the court -- Khaled Daher, Shdeid and Nawfal -- involved vote-counting errors only, the court sources said.
But the Hobeish case appeared more politically sensitive.

Mikhael Daher's petition last September against Hobeish's election said Syria -- which has 35,000 troops in Lebanon and is the country's main power broker -- issued a ban on his re-election at the request of President Elias Hrawi.

Daher's appeal said "the information and security service" -- a code word in Lebanon for Syrian intelligence -- pressured hundreds of key local electoral figures in the Akkar region to support his rival Hobeish.

Daher, a former minister who ran for the presidency against Hrawi in 1988, also cited "flagrant interventions on the part of Lebanese civil and security officials" and said methods used against him and his supporters ranged between "verbal threats and detentions of dozens (of people) for hours in cells under inhumane conditions."
